input.question: Why is water so good at transferring heat?
input.ground_truth: Water has a relatively high [specific heat](_URL_1_), which means that it takes a lot of energy to heat it up (and thus hot water stores a lot of energy). Specific heat is defined (in SI units) as the amount of energy necessary to heat 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree Kelvin. Its units are J/(kg * °C). As a result, a flow of water can carry a substantial amount of heat from one place to another. One of the better-known examples is the [Gulf Stream](_URL_0_) current in the Atlantic Ocean transporting heat northward and warming the climates of the British Isles and Scandinavia. However, it should be noted that water has a relatively low thermal conductivity--the speed at which heat energy will propagate through a material. For heat to transfer through water or a water-based liquid, you generally need a steady current flowing, as in the Gulf Stream or even the blood vessels in the human body.

Okay! Imagine you have a cup of hot chocolate and a cup of ice water. If you put a spoon in both and leave them for a while, the spoon in the hot chocolate will get warm, and the spoon in the ice water will get cold. But if you put the warm spoon into the ice water, the heat from the spoon will go into the water. That’s because water is really good at grabbing onto heat and moving it around.

So, water is like a super helper that picks up heat from one place and takes it to another place really well. That’s why when you sweat, the sweat (which is mostly water) helps your body cool down by carrying heat away from you!
